title: My First Weeks in MDS
text:
My first weeks in UBC’s Master of Data Science program have marked a new chapter after studying statistics and mathematics at the University of Toronto. I am looking forward to building on that background and developing more practical skills in data science. My interests in quantitative finance and machine learning give me a direction to explore as I begin the program.
One of my first impressions of Vancouver has been how much I enjoy the climate here. It has been a pleasant part of the move and has helped make the start of the program feel welcoming. Alongside the academic transition, getting used to a new city is an important part of this experience, and so far Vancouver has left me with a positive impression.
I have also really appreciated the warmth of the TAs and instructors. Their welcoming attitude has made the beginning of MDS feel more comfortable and encouraging. As the program continues, I hope to build my confidence with new tools and connect what I learn to my longer-term interests in quantitative finance and machine learning.



My WeChat avatar, a familiar image accompanying a new chapter at UBC.

title: What Predicts House Sale Prices in Ames?
text:
This short post uses the Ames Housing dataset to fit a simple multiple linear regression model for house sale price. The goal is not to build the best possible prediction model, but to check whether a few basic property features explain a useful amount of variation in prices.
Data: Ames Housing dataset, based on De Cock (2011), “Ames, Iowa: Alternative to the Boston Housing Data as an End of Semester Regression Project.” The AmesHousing package is GPL-2 licensed.
library(ggplot2)

title: What Predicts House Sale Prices in Ames?
text:
Load and select variables
I use sale price as the response variable. The predictors are overall quality, living area, basement area, garage area, lot area, and year built.

ames <- read.csv("AmesHousing.csv")

housing <- data.frame(
  SalePrice = ames$SalePrice,
  Overall_Qual = ames$Overall.Qual,
  Gr_Liv_Area = ames$Gr.Liv.Area,
  Total_Bsmt_SF = ames$Total.Bsmt.SF,
  Garage_Area = ames$Garage.Area,
  Lot_Area = ames$Lot.Area,
  Year_Built = ames$Year.Built
)

housing <- housing[complete.cases(housing), ]

head(housing)

title: What Predicts House Sale Prices in Ames?
text:
Quick summary
The dataset has 2,929 complete rows for these selected variables. Sale prices vary widely, so a regression model should be interpreted as a rough summary rather than a perfect pricing tool.

summary_table <- data.frame(
  homes = nrow(housing),
  mean_price = mean(housing$SalePrice),
  median_price = median(housing$SalePrice),
  mean_living_area = mean(housing$Gr_Liv_Area),
  mean_overall_quality = mean(housing$Overall_Qual)
)

summary_table

  homes mean_price median_price mean_living_area mean_overall_quality
1  2928     180841       160000         1499.784              6.09597

title: What Predicts House Sale Prices in Ames?
text:
Figure
The figure shows a strong positive relationship between above-ground living area and sale price. The colour gradient suggests that overall quality also matters.

ggplot(housing, aes(x = Gr_Liv_Area, y = SalePrice, color = Overall_Qual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(
    x = "Above-ground living area",
    y = "Sale price",
    color = "Overall quality"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 1: Sale price tends to increase with living area, especially for higher-quality homes.

title: What Predicts House Sale Prices in Ames?
text:
Multiple linear regression
The model uses a small set of interpretable predictors. I include log(SalePrice) because house prices are right-skewed and percentage-style changes are easier to interpret.

model <- lm(
  log(SalePrice) ~ Overall_Qual + Gr_Liv_Area + Total_Bsmt_SF +
    Garage_Area + Lot_Area + Year_Built,
  data = housing
)

summary(model)

title: What Predicts House Sale Prices in Ames?
text:
Model diagnostics
The fitted-versus-observed plot shows that the model captures the main price pattern, although expensive homes still have more spread. This is expected for a simple MVLR model with only a few predictors.

housing$fitted_price <- exp(fitted(model))

ggplot(housing, aes(x = fitted_price, y = SalePrice)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Fitted sale price",
    y = "Observed sale price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 2: Observed and fitted sale prices from the multiple linear regression model.

title: What Predicts House Sale Prices in Ames?
text:
Takeaway
Overall quality and living area are the clearest positive predictors in this simple model. Basement size, garage area, lot area, and year built add extra information, but the model is still only a compact summary of prices rather than a full appraisal model.

title: A Python Look at Ames Housing Prices
text:
This post uses the Ames Housing dataset to fit a simple multiple linear regression model in Python. The goal is intentionally modest: use a few easy-to-understand housing features to explain sale price and make a small number of useful plots.
Data: Ames Housing dataset, based on De Cock (2011), “Ames, Iowa: Alternative to the Boston Housing Data as an End of Semester Regression Project.” The AmesHousing package is GPL-2 licensed.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: A Python Look at Ames Housing Prices
text:
Load and prepare data
The response variable is sale price. I use overall quality, living area, basement area, garage area, lot area, and year built as simple predictors.

ames = pd.read_csv("AmesHousing.csv")

housing = ames[[
    "SalePrice",
    "Overall Qual",
    "Gr Liv Area",
    "Total Bsmt SF",
    "Garage Area",
    "Lot Area",
    "Year Built",
]].dropna().copy()

housing.columns = [
    "sale_price",
    "overall_quality",
    "living_area",
    "basement_area",
    "garage_area",
    "lot_area",
    "year_built",
]

Summary table
The selected data have almost all homes in the original file. Sale prices have a high mean relative to the median, suggesting some expensive homes pull the average upward.

summary = pd.DataFrame({

    "median_price": [housing["sale_price"].median()],
    "mean_living_area": [housing["living_area"].mean()],

})

title: A Python Look at Ames Housing Prices
text:
Sale price and living area

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.scatter(housing["living_area"], housing["sale_price"], alpha=0.35)
ax.set_xlabel("Above-ground living area")
ax.set_ylabel("Sale price")
ax.set_title("Sale price vs. living area")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Ames sale price generally increases with above-ground living area.

title: A Python Look at Ames Housing Prices
text:
Multiple linear regression
This model predicts log sale price. I fit the regression with numpy.linalg.lstsq() so the code stays short and does not need an extra modelling package.

predictors = [
    "overall_quality",
    "living_area",
    "basement_area",
    "garage_area",
    "lot_area",
    "year_built",
]

X = housing[predictors].to_numpy()
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])
y = np.log(housing["sale_price"].to_numpy())

coef, residuals, rank, s = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
fitted_log_price = X @ coef

ss_res = np.sum((y - fitted_log_price) ** 2)
ss_tot = np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)
r_squared = 1 - ss_res / ss_tot

coef_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "term": ["Intercept"] + predictors,
    "coefficient": coef,
})

coef_table.round(4), round(r_squared, 3)

title: A Python Look at Ames Housing Prices
text:
Observed vs fitted prices

housing["fitted_price"] = np.exp(fitted_log_price)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.scatter(housing["fitted_price"], housing["sale_price"], alpha=0.35)
low = min(housing["fitted_price"].min(), housing["sale_price"].min())
high = max(housing["fitted_price"].max(), housing["sale_price"].max())
ax.plot([low, high], [low, high], color="red", linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Fitted sale price")
ax.set_ylabel("Observed sale price")
ax.set_title("Observed vs. fitted sale price")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 2: Observed and fitted sale prices from the Python MVLR model.

title: A Python Look at Ames Housing Prices
text:
Takeaway
The Python model tells the same basic story as the R model: overall quality and living area are strong predictors of sale price. The fitted plot shows that a small MVLR can capture the broad price pattern, but there is still variation left over because many housing details are not included.
